channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery — Motorola 68000, Intel 486DX2, AMD Athlon XP, Apple M1, and many more in beautiful detail
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: A “die shot”, as I understand it, is a picture of a computer chip without its outer casing. They are much more amazing-looking than they sound. “A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors.”

item.title: New Online Exhibit Explores North Carolina’s Resistance to the Stamp Act
item.description: North Carolina Department of Natural & Cultural Resources: “The exhibit features more than 60 newly transcribed and searchable historical documents that tell the story of North Carolina’s response to the Stamp Act of 1765, an unpopular British law that sparked protests throughout the American colonies.”

item.title: Update of the FamilySearch Records for India and in Hindu
item.description: Genealogy’s Star: “Some time ago, I posted about the Hindu Pilgrimage Registers (Bahi / Pothi) on the FamilySearch.org website. As time passes the number of records from India have increased. Granted, the number of records is small compared to the population of the country but the addition of records shows that some effort is being made to start more extended collections. This list shows the collections that are now in the FamilySearch Catalog but not the records that are presently in the Images collections of records that are not cataloged or indexed.”

item.title: Chinese Museum to Rise Again: Groundbreaking Follows 2020 Fire
item.description: The Upper West Side Spirit: “It took nearly six full years to accomplish but, finally, the ceremonial groundbreaking was held for the new Museum of Chinese in America (MOCA) on Monday morning Nov. 10. The city-owned building, which stands at 70 Mulberry St. on the northwest corner of Bayard Street suffered significant damage during a nighttime fire on January 23, 2020. It will be rehabilitated and expanded under a $184 million Department of Design and Construction (DDC) reconstruction plan. The expected completion date is 2030.”

item.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
item.description: Ars Technica: “A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week.”

item.title: Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches
item.description: Lifehacker: “Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google’s reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.”

item.title: Sprawling Malware Attack Reportedly Affects Zoom, CNN, Fox News, Peacock, and 170+ Others
item.description: Gizmodo: “Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC, Equifax, and the online outlets of over 170 other brands and companies—many of them familiar—were reportedly serving various kinds of malicious code if you visited them on Monday. Quick caveat: This news about an exploit that implanted malicious scripts comes from Report URI, a company that sells malicious script-detectors, so keep that in mind.”

item.title: A 35 mm film roll in a coal mine: What preserving really means
item.description: Digital Preservation Coalition: “Erick Cardoso Espinoza accompanied Mexico’s deposit at the Arctic World Archive in 2017 as Director of Information Technology at the Archivo General de la Nación. He writes in a personal capacity for World Digital Preservation Day 2026.”

item.title: Engineering team creates 3D-printed raptor puppets to help wildlife rehabilitation
item.description: Western University: “Created through a collaboration with Western Engineering, the 3D-printed puppets resemble a great horned owl, merlin falcon, red-tailed hawk and American kestrel. They are designed to encourage nestlings to associate food with their own species rather than people – an important part of preparing these young patients for a return to the wild.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Students digitize Black women’s history, one diary at a time
item.description: William & Mary: “[Mia] Hunt is one of a dozen W&M students contributing to the Black Women’s Diaries Project (BWDP), a multi‑year effort led by Putzi to transcribe, annotate and digitally encode the diaries of 19th‑ and early 20th‑century African American women.”

item.title: Newly Digitized New York Revolutionary War Records
item.description: New York Almanack: “The first volume of American Revolutionary War Auditor’s Journals held by the New York State Archives are now available online. These journals offer a fascinating look at the day-to-day business of a state in the making, documenting payments to civil and military officers, state agents and employees, legislators, and countless others who provided goods and services during and after the Revolution.”

item.title: New online archive uncovers lost recordings and footage of folk trio Swan Arcade
item.description: Cumberland News and Star: “A major new online archive is shining a spotlight on the legacy of an influential folk group. Swan Arcade, a vocal trio with strong Cumbrian connections, is the focus of a project that brings together rare recordings, forgotten newspaper clippings, and film footage.”

item.title: Bubbles now has Spanish blogs
item.description: Bubbles Blog: “Bubbles has a third edition: bubbles.town/es. It lists about 220 personal blogs written in Spanish, from Spain and from Latin America, with around 2,700 posts so far. Switch to it with the new ES button in the header.”

item.title: Google Docs finally lets you compare Word files without converting them
item.description: Chrome Unboxed: “For years now, Google Docs has let you open, view, and edit Microsoft Office files directly without forcing a format conversion. The catch was that the Compare documents feature still required native Google Docs formatting to track redlines and edits between two versions.”

item.title: There’s a free tool you can use to show what your network is doing, and it takes minutes to set up
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Routers show all your connected devices, but don’t necessarily tell you what they are doing. Your smart TV, phone, and other smart devices could be talking to the internet far more than you expect, and you don’t have easy visibility of this. I tried a free, open-source tool called ntopng that lets me watch what happens live, and it only took a few minutes to install it.”

item.title: Right-wing influencer retracts fraud allegations against Seattle grocery
item.description: Seattle Times: “Nick Shirley, the conservative social media influencer who has been feted at the White House, has retracted viral videos he posted last month in which he accused Lam’s Seafood Asian Market, a small Seattle grocery store, of committing food stamp fraud.”

item.title: They Had 48 Hours to Build Weapons for the Information War
item.description: Under Fire News: “On a campus run by Germany’s armed forces, teams of developers spent a weekend earlier this month hunting bots. They had 48 hours to turn problems in intelligence and information warfare into working tools. By Sunday, one team could flag coordinated accounts automatically, another could map Western companies’ ties to Russia from public records, and a third had built an AI assistant for investigators. That one grew out of its founders’ work investigating crimes committed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.”

item.title: Lightweight web archiving with SingleFile
item.description: Literary Machines: “Web archiving tools today are mature, and easy enough for anybody to curate their own copy of web pages. The simplest approach is ArchiveWeb.page, a Chrome extension that records the web as you browse, and ReplayWeb.page, a web page that plays your recordings back later…. Sometimes, though, I need something simpler and quicker: a single-shot capture, where the full machinery of WARC/WACZ is not necessary. For these cases I often take screenshots, or save the page as HTML from the browser, to keep a local copy of the content (without any archival compliance). Lately I started using the SingleFile extension. ”

item.title: A third of UK businesses on Google Maps have no working website — and many of those that do are struggling to keep them up to date
item.description: TechRadar: “Roughly a third of UK businesses that have claimed their Google listing are sending would-be customers somewhere other than a website they control, and a fair share of the sites that do load look as though nobody has touched them in a while. The findings come from a recent census of Google Business Profile listings published by Digital Royalty, which checked 8,426 open listings across 12 UK towns and cities and 12 everyday business types, from plumbers and electricians to hair salons and accountants.”

item.title: Save Our Data: Preserving At-Risk US Federal Data at the University of Cambridge
item.description: Digital Preservation at the University of Cambridge: “When we talk about digital preservation today, the scope goes beyond scanning historical volumes or maintaining local drives. Modern preservation practices are fundamentally digital, and increasingly, they include open public data. Public datasets form the statistical backbone of modern society — underpinning democratic representation, public infrastructure, and research worldwide.”

item.title: How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation
item.description: Engadget: “Jason Chang was sick of his mother asking him to adjust the family’s solar-powered Christmas lights to get more sun, so he devised a solution with big potential. The 13-year-old seventh grader at Worcester Academy in Massachusetts created a solar tracker that utilizes water and gravity to move a solar panel without the need for a motor, a sunlight sensor or electricity to power the mechanism.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: A New Search Engine Lets You Explore 4 Million Works of Art & Historical Photographs from Museums and Libraries Around the World
item.description: Open Culture: “A constant flow of visual, aural, or textual novelty offers stimulation, to put it mildly, but it inevitably comes to feel insubstantial. However complexly derived from the work of humanity it may be, it lacks a direct connection to that work. Not so the results delivered by Arkivism, a new search engine that responds to descriptions by drawing on a collection of more than four million pieces of real art and photography.”

item.title: Strategic Planning Toolkit & Resource Library for Local History Organizations
item.description: Recollection Wisconsin: “Ready to get to work and plan for the future? The Wisconsin Historical Society and WiLS have created a Strategic Planning Toolkit & Resource Library to help local history organizations turn ideas into action. Explore practical guidance, videos, worksheets, and hands-on activities that break strategic planning into manageable steps. You can also find templates, examples, and other resources to help develop a plan that reflects your organization’s mission, goals, and future.”

item.title: Your choice: Turn AI answers on or off in Bing
item.description: Bing Blogs: “AI is doing powerful things for search, and our research shows users want to have the option to choose whether or not AI is involved in every session. Sometimes a quick AI-generated summary is exactly what you need. Other times, you’d rather scan the results, compare sources and decide for yourself what information to trust. We’re proud of the AI experiences we’re building in Bing. Being able to turn AI answers off when you want to isn’t a step back from AI. It’s a step toward putting you in charge of how you use it.”

item.title: Scammers stole his image to lure the lovesick. Then the lovesick came looking for him
item.description: Associated Press: “For more than eight years, romance scammers have stolen Hunter [Bigham]’s photos to create hundreds of fake online profiles that have been used to trick lovesick men and women out of their money. When many victims realize they’ve been duped, they dig — eventually finding Hunter. The losses he’s tallied just from victims who have contacted him have reached roughly $1.4 million.”

item.title: Jordan bans Telegram app over ‘extremism and radicalism’ concerns
item.description: The National: “Jordan banned the Telegram messaging app on Monday, saying it could be used to promote ‘extremism and radicalism’….Officials did not link the platform to a deadly attack on an Orthodox church last month. But the ban came a day after three men were sentenced to death for killing nine people and wounding more than 30 in that attack.”

item.title: New York forces T-Mobile to remove 50GB cap that throttled low-income home internet users to 600Kbps
item.description: TechSpot: “Cheap home internet isn’t much use if it slows to a crawl a few days into the month. New York says that’s exactly what T-Mobile was offering low-income households, imposing a 50GB monthly cap before slashing download speeds to under 1 Mbps. The carrier has now agreed to remove the restriction after state investigators found it violated the Affordable Broadband Act.”

item.title: Euclid lays the foundation for its best-ever 3D map of the Universe
item.description: European Space Agency: “The European Space Agency’s Euclid mission has released its first major batch of data. With this release, which captures the light of more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky as big as 9500 full Moons, ESA’s dark Universe detective lays the foundation for its largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos.”

item.title: Science Museum of Minnesota Makes Difficult Cuts to Balance Budget, Says Community Investment Now Critical to Its Future
item.description: Science Museum of Minnesota: “Like cultural institutions nationwide, especially science centers, the Science Museum has faced sustained pressure in recent years. Attendance has not returned to pre-pandemic levels, and revenue from the museum’s touring exhibitions, historically a significant source of income, has declined as other museums face the same constraints. Federal and state funding for the museum’s science and education work was cut by nearly 80%. Meanwhile, the costs of operating and maintaining the museum’s large riverfront building continue to rise.”

item.title: A ‘living’ wall could help buildings breathe easier
item.description: Yale University: “A new Yale-led study demonstrates the promising potential of plant-based systems to remove carbon dioxide (CO₂) from indoor settings, an innovation that would decrease human exposure to the ubiquitous gas and help maintain healthier building environments as atmospheric levels of CO2 rise.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: People called this Elora, Ont., company for a washer it supposedly sells. Except it doesn’t even make washers
item.description: CBC: “The video suggested the ‘bombshell washer’ by Stirling Marathon would disrupt North America’s washer industry. It would be good news for any other business, except the Elora, Ont., appliance maker doesn’t even sell washers. The Ontario business featured in a recent scam powered by artificial intelligence, where someone posted a YouTube video combining real company marketing images with AI-generated content to advertise a fictional washer called ‘the Keel.'”

item.title: Prestigious Traver Award nearly hijacked by AI
item.description: Hatch: “Artificial intelligence owes a couple of renowned fly-fishing writers a deeply legitimate apology. After being passed over by an AI-generated piece submitted by Romanian ‘author’ Andrei Romanov, real human writers were rightfully recognized by the John D. Voelker Foundation and the American Museum of Fly Fishing last month when the legit winner in the annual Robert Traver Fly Fishing-Writing Award was announced after the AI winner was rightfully disqualified.”

item.title: Data centers go 0-for-21 in ballot initiatives around Ohio
item.description: Ohio Capital Journal: “Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. Around Ohio, 18 communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center developments. In all 18 communities, voters decided that, yes, that would be a good idea.”

item.title: Alaska DNR OKs scaled-down land transfer for data center development near Houston
item.description: The Alaska Current: “The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a scaled-down version of a controversial land transfer to a state-owned corporation, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority. According to a final finding and decision published Tuesday afternoon, DNR has approved a plan that would give approximately 6,800 of land for free to the state-owned corporation. That’s less than the 19,500 acres that had been earmarked for transfer in a preliminary July decision.”

item.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
item.description: The Register: “Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it’s needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing.”

item.title: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand
item.description: Futurism: “Paradium.AI, the recently-rebranded media company formerly known as The Arena Group, announced staggering third-quarter losses yesterday as it continues to go ‘all in’ on AI. Paradium’s stock has been declining for years, though it experienced a drop of about 14 percent today after the company revealed that it had sustained a net loss of $3.6 million in the Q3 of 2026 — a dramatic shift from the same quarter last year, when its revenue was around 30 percent higher and it logged a $6.9 million net profit.”

item.title: What Is Shadow AI, and How Can Federal Agencies Manage It?
item.description: FedTech: “Federal workers are eager to put artificial intelligence to work, and they aren’t waiting for permission. Roughly 27% of government professionals report using unsanctioned AI tools, and that poses new risks: A National Cybersecurity Alliance survey found 43% of AI users have shared sensitive information with AI tools without their employer’s knowledge. This ‘shadow AI’ requires both a new approach to governance and new tools for identifying IT resources. What’s needed is not prohibition, but guidance.”

item.title: South Korea races to curb AI cheating ahead of college entrance exam
item.description: Korea Herald: “An Education Ministry official sat in front of reporters Monday, looking down at a mock exam paper before tapping the side of his glasses. Within moments, the artificial intelligence-powered device began processing the question, demonstrating how a student could use the glasses to seek answers without speaking a word.”

item.title: Designing Research Assignments in the AI Era
item.description: Wake Forest University: “If you’ve also been wondering about research projects in the AI era, Kathy and Amanda hosted a First Five: ZSR Early Career Faculty Workshop on this topic. What we’ve included below is a snapshot of our five key recommendations, which range from looking at the ‘big picture’ of why we assign research assignments to practical strategies you can implement in assignment design.”

item.title: The Apple Watch’s New ‘Siri Recap’ Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected
item.description: Lifehacker: “The ‘Siri Recap’ feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the ‘Live Rewind’ feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.”

item.title: Inside the First AI Music Awards, a Chaotic Evening Attempting to Normalize Tech-Assisted Tunes
item.description: Variety: “To qualify for the awards, artists needed to register their tracks to SIQA’s ‘Verified Registry,’ which denotes whether the song was fully AI-generated, made with the assistance of AI or featured a cloned human voice to lead the tune (what the group calls a ‘human + AI hybrid’).”

item.title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
item.description: The Guardian: “Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found. A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.”

item.title: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.
item.description: NiemanLab: “For our new report, ‘Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,’ we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.”

item.title: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
item.description: PsyPost: “People tend to perceive artificial intelligence systems as White, even when those systems lack a face, voice, name, or body, according to new research published in Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Across a series of studies, this racial association was linked to greater trust in AI recommendations, and systems described as trained on data from Black and Latino adults were assigned less intellectually demanding work than identical systems trained on White or unspecified data.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New Digital Editions of Hegel, Schelling
item.description: Daily Nous: “Giuliano Infantino, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Toronto, has created new, freely accessible digital editions of the works of Hegel and Schelling.”

item.title: Preserving 30 Years of Salon Journalism
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been preserving Salon for nearly three decades—the online publication has been published over time at salon1999.com, salonmag.com and, since 1999, salon.com. Today, more than 250,000 Salon articles can be discovered through the Wayback Machine, representing a record of digital journalism and the conversations that shaped our culture since the earliest days of the web. To make exploring this web archive easier, we’ve also launched an experimental Salon Explorer, a new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism.”

item.title: Buro Media Launches Database of Lukashenko’s Inner Circle
item.description: OCCRP: “OCCRP’s Belarusian member center Buro Media has launched a database profiling 20 people close to Aleksandr Lukashenko, documenting their assets, business interests, connections, and privileges.”

item.title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
item.description: Associated Press: “The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.”

item.title: Moving your site used to mean starting over. Not anymore
item.description: WordPress: “Moving to WordPress.com now brings your design with you, too. Paste your site’s address, and we bring your pages, images, and design over as a WordPress site you own. Have a website on Squarespace, Wix, Lovable, Base44, or another builder? Your site’s address is all you need to get started. No files to download, nothing to rebuild.”

item.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
item.description: The Register: “eMudhra’s private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it – and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television.”

item.title: How to Make Interactive Maps for Free
item.description: Maps Mania: “You don’t need an expensive subscription to Google Maps, Mapbox or Esri to create your own interactive web maps. There is a growing collection of free, open-source tools that allow you to build sophisticated, customised maps that can be published online without paying for mapping software or map tiles.”

item.title: Introducing Reference Drawer – A Tool for Organizing Your Reference Images
item.description: Kai Gulliksen: “Simply, you point the app at a folder of your choice and it displays all the images contained in that folder. From there you can apply tags and view the images in full size. The app also comes with a built-in Mood Board feature so you can create separate reference boards using the images from your gallery.”

item.title: Alaska proposal could tighten access to state records in Juneau
item.description: Juneau Empire: “Proposed changes to Alaska’s public records rules could make it harder for Juneau residents to access information about state government decisions by allowing agencies to stop processing requests after 15 hours of work or reviewing 250 records.”

item.title: Zelenskyy says Starshield has been slowed again, endangering Ukraine’s defense
item.description: Engadget: “As media headlines focus on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the midterms fallout, you could almost forget that Ukraine is still fighting for its life — with all of Europe nervously watching. According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, his job just got harder again. The country’s access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, has been hit with ‘systematic speed restrictions’ for several days.”

item.title: Tools and Workflows I Use For Blogging With Low Vision
item.description: Veronica With Four Eyes: “None of this would be possible without my amazing readers and the technology that enables me to write and share free resources about low vision assistive technology here on Veroniiiica. Here is an overview of the tools and workflows I use for blogging and maintaining my website with low vision, perfect for anyone who wants to start their own blog! Since this an anniversary post, I also included a few highlights and stories from writing Veroniiiica over the years.”

item.title: Virtual Reading Room Service Extends Access to Archival Collections
item.description: University of California San Francisco: “The VRR enables researchers to consult collections that cannot be made openly available online due to technical, privacy and copyright-related restrictions. Developed in partnership with UCSF Academic Research Services’ Research Analysis Environment (RAE), this tool enables researchers to remotely view and analyze archival materials via their web browser and without a visit our onsite reading room.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: CIDRAP database tracks more than 150 coronavirus vaccines for animals
item.description: DVM360: “Entries are built from publicly available information and cover vaccines for domesticated animals that are either in development or commercially available. More than 150 candidates were in the database at launch. As of November 11, the CIDRAP tracker listed 156 candidates across 11 viruses, 13 vaccine platforms, and 7 animal species.”

item.title: New update to the Unplanned Explosions at Munitions Sites database
item.description: Small Arms Survey: “Unplanned explosions at munitions sites (UEMS) are a significant safety threat for states and their citizens, and a major challenge for the international community. A single UEMS incident can result in multiple casualties, millions of dollars’ worth of damage to nearby buildings, infrastructure, and homes, as well as harm to the environment…. The Survey’s November 2026 UEMS database update includes data up to 30 June 2026, and highlights that between January 1979 and June 2026, almost 700 UEMS incidents and 32,000 resulting casualties were recorded.”

item.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage
item.description: Associated Press: “Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours…. Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.”

item.title: Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10
item.description: 9to5 Google: “After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.”

item.title: The foreign influencers helping Russia sell its occupation
item.description: Kyiv Independent: “The tour of Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast offered visitors a carefully staged portrayal of life under Russian rule. Experts told the Kyiv Independent that the visit was part of a broader effort to whitewash Russia’s international image, legitimize its occupation and turn the visitors into unwitting amplifiers of Russian propaganda.”

item.title: TikTok launches initiative to promote Philippine heritage sites through livestreams
item.description: ABS-CBN: “TikTok has launched an initiative with the UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines (UNACOM) and the Department of Tourism (DOT) to promote the country’s historical and cultural landmarks through livestreaming, as it explores new ways to bring heritage closer to younger audiences.”

item.title: Free Speech Nonprofit Says US to End Efforts to Curb Facebook Group and App Reporting ICE Activity
item.description: Reuters: “Free speech ⁠group ⁠FIRE said on Friday ⁠the US government agreed to end efforts to press ​Apple and Facebook to restrict platforms created by two Americans reporting Immigration and ‌Customs Enforcement activity.”

item.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
item.description: The Register: “Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK’s Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.”

item.title: Sector warned of ‘acute threat’ posed by AI scraping bots
item.description: Museums Association: “AI scraping poses substantial and unsustainable costs on cultural heritage institutions, which are ‘existential to the mission of these bodies’. That’s the warning from a new white paper for policymakers based on research conducted by the University of Edinburgh in 2026 as part of the Ekip (European Cultural and Creative Sectors and Industries Policy Platform) project.”

item.title: New report claims TikTok Live is fastest-growing platform for game streaming
item.description: Tubefilter: “Hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Digital archives unveiled, offering L-V history to all
item.description: Leader-Vindicator: “Through a partnership among the Redbank Valley Public Library, The Leader-Vindicator, Redbank Valley Historical Society, Clarion Free Library and the Eccles-Lesher Memorial Library in Rimersburg, past issues of The Leader-Vindicator — as well as its predecessors, the New Bethlehem Vindicator and New Bethlehem Leader — can be accessed for free online.”

item.title: The first digital archive of Sant Antoni is born, with the history and traditions of all the towns of Mallorca
item.description: ARA Balears: “The most celebrated festival in Mallorca, Sant Antoni, now has its own space on the internet that aims to become the shared archive of the celebration on the island. The website… was born with the intention of gathering in one single portal the history, programs, images, music, and the peculiarities of the festival in all the towns of the island.”

item.title: Visualizing the Oscars: An Interactive Data Visualization Website
item.description: Post-Machina: “I have created a website from scratch using Claude-generated code and human-structured data using nomination trends at the Academy Awards from 2009 to 2025 as my basis!”

item.title: The FAA nationwide ground stop sparks travel panic and viral memes
item.description: Mashable: “Of course, this being the internet, it didn’t take long for people to find humor in the situation, either. Even an unprecedented disruption to air travel isn’t immune to a few jokes, particularly when it happens on Friday the 13th following a major Microsoft outage.”

item.title: LinkedIn is testing a Frequent Viewer tool to snitch on professional stalkers
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Every single day, I get an email or two telling me who visited my LinkedIn profile. It has almost become a fun daily routine, and I often joke to myself that life might occasionally throw me a curveball, but LinkedIn’s ‘who viewed your profile’ emails will always arrive on time. Whether or not you like these emails, LinkedIn is now testing a new ‘frequent viewer’ label that tells you if someone is repeatedly visiting your profile.”

item.title: Setting Up fediverse:creator Tags With The SEO Framework
item.description: The New Leaf Journal: “Below, I will highlight new Fediverse-related features in the free and open source The SEO Framework plugin for WordPress. This article piggybacks off an earlier article I wrote about configuring fediverse:creator tags in WordPress with the help of the Simple fediverse:creator plugin, so I will begin with a brief summary of my first post before moving on to the main topic.”

item.title: Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase
item.description: The Register: “Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students’ mailboxes. The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions’ first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028.”

item.title: Uber confirms hackers stole thousands of drivers’ license information in data breach
item.description: TechCrunch: “Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.”

item.title: Pentagon sued over failures to make military review boards’ decisions accessible
item.description: Federal News Network: “A nonprofit legal advocacy group representing service members and veterans is suing the Defense Department and President Donald Trump, saying the military has failed to make the decisions of the services’ Discharge Review Boards and Boards for Correction of Military Records accessible to the public, as required by law.”

item.title: South Korea to accelerate digitization and access to North Korea data
item.description: Chosun Biz: “The digitization of North Korea–related materials and the building of databases are expected to accelerate. The Ministry of Unification will expand and relocate the North Korea Materials Center inside the National Library of Korea in Seocho-gu, Seoul, into the Northeast Asia Peace Resource Center early next year. It will also build a digital archive so researchers can view North Korea materials online.”

item.title: Next generation of military scans archives for clues to missing service members
item.description: North Dakota Monitor: “Bella Hammer, a social work student and member of the North Dakota Air National Guard, regularly supports military-affiliated students as part of her work with the University of North Dakota’s Veteran & Military Services. She recently found a new way to serve veterans when she played a role in an archival project.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: “Naming Names at the Highest Level”
item.description: National Security Archive: “The Embassy’s report on ‘Narcotics Trafficking in Colombia and Related High Level Corruption’ is among 50 previously classified documents published today by the Archive to mark 50 years since the U.S. government began to look seriously at narcotics-related corruption in Colombia. Together, these records provide vivid new details on the sequence of events that led President Carter to confront the Colombian President with evidence that members of his own government benefitted from the illegal drug trade.”

item.title: Celebrity.Estate Launches Interactive World Map of Famous Wills and Inheritance Cases From Caesar to 2026
item.description: EIN Presswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “Celebrity.estate has launched a public online archive of celebrity estates, famous wills, inheritance disputes and family fortunes from 40,000 BC to 2026. The archive places each case on an animated world map at the place and year it happened. Each case page cites its sources, with court records listed first.”

item.title: Top Million Sites Lost 12% Of Visits; Top 100’s Share Barely Moved
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro. The proportion of visits that go to websites that are not among the top 100 stayed relatively consistent over this time. That means while the total number of visits was down, that proportion still added up to less traffic for non-top-100 sites.”

item.title: Government plans national digital archive and cultural ambassador programme
item.description: The Sun: “The Turks and Caicos Islands Government has announced plans to establish a National Digital Archive, an Artisan Registry and a National Cultural Ambassador Programme as part of efforts to preserve the country’s cultural heritage, promote traditional skills and strengthen national identity.”

item.title: Firefox’s free built-in VPN uncaps data limit through January 2027
item.description: Mozilla Blog: “Whether you’re heading home to see family this winter or taking a well-earned break before the year wraps up, we want you to browse with a little more peace of mind. That’s why, as our gift to you, everyone using Firefox’s free built-in VPN gets unlimited data starting today, November 10, through January 31, 2027. Sign in with a Mozilla account and unlock extra privacy for all that shopping, travel planning, and everyday browsing, no gift receipt required.”

item.title: Google clears key map security checks in Korea, taps Tmap as local partner
item.description: Korea Herald: “South Korea on Friday confirmed that Google had implemented key security measures required to export detailed Korean map data, bringing the US tech giant a step closer to offering full navigation services after nearly two decades of regulatory hurdles.”

item.title: Influencer high fived Ariana Grande at the NYC Marathon, then a man who waited 10 years to get in saw the photos and recognized his own bib number
item.description: We Got This Covered: “Content creator Mike Clarke is banned from the 2027 New York City Marathon after organizers said he used a counterfeit race bib to run in this year’s event, as reported by Dexerto. Clarke completed the full 26.2-mile course even though he never officially registered for the race…..The bib number he wore, 4207, belonged to Nicolas Bourot, the chief security officer for the French banking group BPCE. Bourot said he had spent 10 years trying to get a spot in the race.”

item.title: EU ‘Digital Fairness Act’ Could Have A Huge Impact On Loot Boxes And Virtual Currency
item.description: Nintendo Life: “To be clear, the proposal has not been adopted by the EU Commission just yet, but if it does go through, it could have a huge impact on several hot-topic game mechanics like loot boxes, virtual currencies, pay-to-win options and more. What’s more, the act would apply to all EU member states without the need for individual approval.”

item.title: Could new mathematics help the internet carry more data through existing cables?
item.description: Aston University: “Aston University researchers have been awarded almost £500,000 to investigate whether new mathematical techniques could help existing fibre-optic cables carry more data, potentially reducing the need for costly investment in new infrastructure.”

item.title: Ireland can learn from Brazil’s victory over disinformation
item.description: Irish Examiner: “We should know who is behind the largest social media platforms — because once we do, we quickly understand why misinformation is one of the main problems we face today. Their algorithms weaponise engagement, amplifying fake news while shielding executive boards from accountability. In Brazil, democratic survival depended on citizens recognising a stark truth: tech giants and political elites will not save us — and maybe that was the best realisation for us Brazilians.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New Planetary Society study finds that NASA’s cheapest science missions can’t replace larger ones
item.description: The Planetary Society: “[The Planetary Society’s new Science Mission Impact dashboard] tracks 143 NASA-led science missions launched from 1980 through 2024, across all five science divisions, along with their inflation-adjusted costs and 148,667 peer-reviewed papers associated with them.”

item.title: Hicky’s Bengal Gazette now fully digitised and accessible online
item.description: PrintWeek: “Scholars, historians, and journalism enthusiasts can now access every surviving page of India’s first-ever newspaper, Hicky’s Bengal Gazette… The digital archive was announced by author and researcher Andrew Otis, who spent years tracking down historical editions. For the first time in history, a complete run of the publication has been brought together in a single, searchable online platform.”

item.title: Starting in the 18th century: Database lists 1,900 Swiss banks
item.description: Blue News: “A new database has compiled information on approximately 1,900 banks that have existed in Switzerland since the 18th century. This historical analysis reveals a steady structural transformation, from phases of establishment to phases of consolidation, over the course of three centuries.”

item.title: Microsoft reports progress in reviving email and other services during a global outage
item.description: Associated Press: “Microsoft said progress is being made in bringing its popular workplace software back online as a global outage enters its second day, disrupting business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and many other services.”

item.title: WordPress 7.2 Beta 5
item.description: WordPress: “WordPress 7.2 Beta 5 continues refining the upcoming release with additional security, accessibility, and compatibility improvements. Recent changes include email notifications when application passwords are created, improved keyboard navigation in the WordPress admin toolbar, and accessibility refinements to Visual History.”

item.title: Encyclopedia Of Chicago Goes Offline As History Museum Seeks To Upgrade Site
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “Almost anyone doing online research on the history of the city has come across the Encyclopedia of Chicago, an invaluable resource that chronicles nearly four centuries of the city and region’s past. But in September, the site — the digital version of a 1,117-page print book — was taken down as the Chicago History Museum seeks to upgrade the technology behind it.”

item.title: I discovered a free retro TV app built from the Internet Archive’s forgotten VHS recordings, and I can’t stop watching it
item.description: XDA Developers: ” I’m a sucker for nostalgia, so when I stumbled across a Reddit post about Spelunkr, a streaming service that clearly aims to recreate the vibe of old-school cable TV, I couldn’t help but check it out. An entirely free app that streams content I watched as a kid is right up my alley.”

item.title: Introducing Google Fi’s new super network
item.description: Google Blog: “Google Fi Wireless is launching our new super network, automatically switching you between two of America’s best 5G cellular networks and millions of premium Wi-Fi networks.”

item.title: North Korean hackers steal more than $400 million using video images, FBI says
item.description: Reuters: “North Korean state-backed hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using surreptitiously recorded images of people which are then used to target their contacts, the FBI said Thursday. As part of a social engineering scheme, which the FBI refers to as ‘FaceStealer,’ targets are lured to video chats on imposter versions of video meeting software such as Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet.”

item.title: Pirate Library WeLib Hit With $19.5m Default Judgment and Domain Takedown Order
item.description: TorrentFreak: “A New York federal judge has awarded thirteen major publishers $19.5 million in damages in their lawsuit against pirate library WeLib. The default judgment also orders registries, registrars and hosting providers, including Cloudflare and Njalla, to take the site’s domains offline. Whether the publishers will ever see any money is doubtful, as WeLib’s operators have yet to be identified.”

item.title: Social media algorithms on X promote content that conflicts with your values
item.description: PsyPost: “Research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals that the feed algorithm on the platform prioritizes content that conflicts with users’ explicit beliefs. The researchers suggest this dynamic may be driven by users replying to posts they dislike, a habit that appears to disproportionately affect left-leaning users.”

item.title: Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor’s entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — ‘You’re right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,’ humbled agent admits
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases.”

item.title: “Ram Altman” Is Now a Linux Script That Emails Sam Altman Daily to Report How Much Unused RAM Is in Your PC
item.description: Respawn First: “Open-source developer Iain Kay has created an open-source BASH script called ‘Ram Altman’ for Linux systems designed to monitor how much idle RAM you have sitting on your rigs, laptops, etc. The percentage of unused RAM is than emailed to Sam Altman… well not really. The correspondence depends on how you set it up. By default, the email server isn’t set up out of the box.”

item.title: SpaceX Plans $74 Billion Investment to Build Data Centers in Texas and Arizona
item.description: New York Times: “SpaceX said on Thursday that it planned to invest $74 billion to build new data center campuses in Arizona and Texas as the company continued to pour money into the global artificial intelligence race. The projects, proposed by Elon Musk’s rocket and A.I. company, would be among some of the largest data center projects in the United States.”

item.title: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
item.description: The Guardian: “Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.”

item.title: Claude Code token cost explorer
item.description: Entropic Thoughts: “I tried some existing tools like ccusage and claude-agent-ledger, but they weren’t able to give me the sort of breakdown into specifics I needed to optimise my usage. Thus, I shamelessly had Claude Code whip up a tool that gives me a better view of its token usage.” This article is aggressively footnoted; a footnote was omitted from this quote.

item.title: How AI is shifting the face of journalism, causing a “crisis” in the media industry
item.description: Northeastern University: “Microsoft and Barclays are among some of the latest companies that have announced thousands of job cuts linked to their implementation of AI. British publishers Reach and Future announced hundreds of layoffs in recent months as some readers rely on AI summaries instead of clicking on complete articles. Journalists have emphasized the value of humans gathering and confirming the accuracy of information as opposed to the AI collection of often unconfirmed commentary available on the internet.”

item.title: North Carolina Department of Information Technology looking for AI vendors
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “From accessing state services online to the technology government employees use behind the scenes, artificial intelligence could soon play a bigger role in how North Carolina operates.”

item.title: School buses are becoming AI-powered ticket machines, generating millions from drivers who fail to stop
item.description: TechSpot: “An investigation by Bloomberg and Type Investigations earlier this year reported that BusPatrol equipped around 35,000 buses across 24 states. Its cameras flag suspected illegal passing, with police reviewing evidence before tickets are issued. In Montgomery County, Maryland, the investigation tallied more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in issued fines. Those are some stunning figures, but the research found little reduction in violations and no evidence of fewer collisions near stopped buses.”

item.title: Is that advertisement AI-generated? These 6 signs offer clues.
item.description: Mashable: “In a September study of more than 500 consumers, only 17 percent correctly identified the AI-generated ad in a lineup of 10 — even though half initially felt confident they could spot it. So what gives an AI ad away? Often, it’s something small that doesn’t hold up as well as the overall image. These six signs can offer clues.”

item.title: As brands dive into ChatGPT, OpenAI will let them track their mentions
item.description: Tubefilter: “If AI chatbots are going to remain a relevant touchpoint for marketers, then agencies and brands need access to the same analytics they use in their other campaigns. Rumor has it that OpenAI is developing new tools in that area, potentially creating new opportunities for advertisers on ChatGPT.”

item.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
item.description: The Register: “OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these.” I wish I could put meme responses here sometimes.

item.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
item.description: Ars Technica: “Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.”

item.title: Stevens INI researchers use generative AI to fill gaps in brain wiring maps
item.description: University of Southern California: “Researchers from the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that helps fill gaps in brain wiring maps made with diffusion MRI, a type of scan that traces the brain’s nerve fiber pathways. This could help researchers study how key brain connections change with aging and disease.”
